prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [adversarial] Long headers over tiny numbers (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Site" · longest unbreakable word 28px · one-line width 28px
  col 2: header "Average weekly active users across all platforms" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 347px
  col 3: header "Median session length in minutes" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 238px
  col 4: header "Share of sessions that ended in a purchase" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 307px
  col 5: header "Number of support tickets opened" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 246px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 593px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 592px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Compare site activity, session duration, purchase conversion and support demand across three sites.","reading":"Read each row as a site profile and scan down each metric to compare sites; the long headers will determine header height while the short body values leave ample space.","groups":["Columns 2 and 3 describe activity and engagement; column 4 describes conversion; column 5 describes support demand. All four are comparable site metrics, while column 1 identifies each row."],"keep_intact":["Site identifiers A, B and C","Numeric values and their suffixes","Individual words in headers"],"may_wrap":["The four metric headers can wrap at spaces; their shared header row can absorb multiple lines."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r2A: widths [50, 160, 115, 145, 122] · table 593×216px · row heights [106, 36, 36, 36] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2B: widths [50, 150, 115, 155, 122] · table 593×216px · row heights [106, 36, 36, 36] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2C: widths [50, 150, 130, 140, 122] · table 593×216px · row heights [106, 36, 36, 36] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
